hypothesis: Organizations that regularly run structured AI-misinformation tabletop exercises, live simulations, and scoped red-team engagements will demonstrate measurably faster, more coordinated, and more effective responses to simulated AI-driven misinformation incidents than organizations that rely solely on static documentation and one-off briefings.

baseline.name: Static-Playbook Readiness Check
baseline.description: Assess organizational readiness using existing documentation and ad hoc discussions only. No facilitated tabletop exercises, no scripted simulations, and no formal red-team challenge are conducted during the test window.
procedures: Collect current AI-misinformation related artifacts: incident response plans, playbooks, escalation matrices, comms templates, governance charters.

Run a 60–90 minute briefing with the core incident response group (comms, brand, risk, legal, security, HR as applicable) to walk through a single written scenario at a high level without time-boxed decisions or injects.
Administer a standardized self-assessment survey immediately after the briefing to capture perceived readiness, clarity of roles, and confidence in decision thresholds.

Run a controlled, time-boxed **baseline simulation** using the provided repository scripts (e.g., `simulations/baseline_run.py`) that simulates an AI-misinformation incident with minimal facilitation and without prior structured practice. Capture response timing, decision quality, and coordination metrics as defined under `metrics`.
Record all metrics via the `evidence_schema` and store raw logs, timestamps, and decisions for later comparison with the treatment condition.

treatment.name: Structured Exercise & Red-Team Program
treatment.description: Introduce a structured, repeatable program comprising executive tabletop exercises, live simulations with scripted injects, and a bounded red-team adversarial exercise, then re-run the same standardized simulation used in the baseline to measure improvement.
procedures: Design 2–3 tabletop exercise scenarios using the scenario templates in the repository (e.g., `scenarios/deepfake_exec_call.yaml`, `scenarios/review_bombing.yaml`), tailored to the organization’s crown-jewel trust assets and channels.

Conduct at least one 2–3 hour executive tabletop exercise and one cross-functional tabletop exercise within a 4–6 week window. Use facilitation guides and inject timelines from `exercises/tabletop_guides/`.

Run at least one live simulation using the repository’s simulation engine (e.g., `simulations/live_timeline_sim.py`) in which synthetic social posts, media inquiries, and internal alerts are released over a compressed timeline. Require participants to interact via their usual collaboration tools (chat, ticketing, email) where feasible.

Conduct a bounded red-team exercise (e.g., 1–2 days) where an internal or external red team uses the scenario generators (e.g., `redteam/generator.ipynb`) to craft adversarial AI-misinformation narratives under pre-agreed rules of engagement (no real-world posting, sandbox-only assets). The blue team responds according to current playbooks.

After each exercise, run a structured debrief and After-Action Review (AAR) using templates from `exercises/debrief_templates/`. Update playbooks, escalation matrices, and comms drafts as remediation actions.

Within 2 weeks after the last exercise, re-run the same standardized simulation used in the baseline (same scenario configuration and initial conditions) and capture the same metrics: time-to-detect, time-to-first-executive-brief, decision clarity, coordination quality, and outcome alignment with policy.
Collect follow-up self-assessment survey responses to measure changes in perceived readiness and clarity, using identical questions as in the baseline.

workloads.name: Workload A: Executive Tabletop Exercise
workloads.description: A facilitated, discussion-based tabletop exercise for senior leaders focused on strategic decisions, escalation thresholds, and external messaging in response to a high-impact AI-misinformation incident.
participants: General Counsel or senior legal representative
Business unit leader(s) relevant to the scenario
workloads.scenario_input: Select one high-impact scenario YAML/JSON configuration from `scenarios/` (e.g., synthetic deepfake of CEO making false market-moving comments) and parameterize for your industry and geography.

timeline.execution: 120–180 minutes session with scripted injects every 10–20 minutes.
timeline.debrief: 30–45 minutes immediate hot-wash plus additional 60 minutes AAR within 5 business days.

procedure: Load the chosen scenario config file (e.g., `scenarios/deepfake_exec_call.yaml`) into the facilitator notebook (`exercises/facilitator_console.ipynb`).
Brief participants on ground rules (no blame, focus on decisions, time-boxed responses).
Execute the tabletop according to the timeline, introducing injects (media queries, social amplification, regulator interest, employee questions) via slides or printed cards.
Time-box key decisions (e.g., 5–10 minutes) and record who decides, what is decided, and rationales.
Capture timestamps of simulated detection, first executive briefing, public response decision, and coordination actions.
Run a structured hot-wash using the AAR template; collect qualitative notes on confusion points, gaps in playbooks, and disagreements.

workloads.name: Workload B: Live Simulation with Synthetic Information Flow
workloads.description: A more operational simulation where cross-functional responders interact with a scripted but dynamic stream of synthetic social media content, press queries, and internal alerts over a compressed timeline using a simulation engine.
participants: Operational comms and social media team members
Brand management and customer support representatives
workloads.scenario_input: Select one scenario config designed for live simulation (e.g., `scenarios/review_bombing_campaign.yaml` or `scenarios/fake_safety_incident.yaml`) and configure intensity and duration parameters.

timeline.prep: 3–4 hours to configure simulation parameters in `simulations/live_timeline_sim.py` or `simulations/live_timeline_sim.ipynb` and test delivery channels.
timeline.execution: 90–150 minutes live run with injects scheduled every 2–5 minutes of real time.
timeline.debrief: 60–90 minutes AAR within 48 hours of simulation end.

procedure: Configure the simulation file with chosen parameters: attack start time, channels (e.g., Twitter-like, messaging app, news site), adversary behavior (escalation rate), and noise level.
Map simulated channels to real collaboration tools (e.g., send simulated social posts to a dedicated Slack channel, press inquiries via email, internal rumors via chat).
Start the simulation and log all generated events and timestamps to `data/logs/<org>_sim_run_{timestamp}.jsonl`.
Require participants to use their standard operating procedures: create tickets, draft responses, escalate incidents, and document decisions in their usual tools.
Use the facilitator console to pause or accelerate the simulation if needed while keeping a record of any timeline modifications.
At the end of the run, export all logs and decisions; generate an automatic timeline reconstruction using `analytics/build_timeline.ipynb` as input to the AAR.

workloads.name: Workload C: Scoped Red-Team Exercise
workloads.description: A controlled adversarial exercise where a designated red team designs and launches synthetic AI-misinformation campaigns inside a sandbox environment to probe weaknesses in monitoring, governance, and response playbooks.
participants: Red team: 2–4 individuals (internal security, external consultants, or cross-functional staff) briefed on AI-misinformation tactics and the scenario generator.
Blue team: Existing misinformation incident responders (comms, security, legal, risk, product, customer support).
White cell / control: 1–2 facilitators responsible for safety, logging, and adherence to rules of engagement.
workloads.scenario_input: Use the red-team scenario generator notebook (e.g., `redteam/generator.ipynb`) with organization-specific parameters (brands, key execs, product names, channels) but restricted to sandboxed assets and non-public channels.

timeline.prep: 1–2 days to define scope, rules of engagement, success conditions, and to generate/red-team assets.
timeline.execution: 1–2 days for multi-phase adversarial exercise (multiple campaigns or escalations).
timeline.debrief: Half-day (3–4 hours) AAR with both red and blue teams.

procedure: Define and document rules of engagement in `redteam/roe_template.md` including forbidden tactics (e.g., no real-world posting, no targeting actual customers), allowed vectors (internal test channels, synthetic datasets), and safety checks.

Use the generator notebook to produce synthetic artifacts: fake but realistic social posts, deepfake thumbnails, fabricated news headlines, and email inquiries. Store them in a clearly-labeled sandbox directory.
Schedule and coordinate the attack phases with the white cell; configure monitoring tools (if any) to ingest sandboxed events as if they were real.
Allow the red team to launch campaigns at pre-agreed windows while white cell logs all injects, detection points, and responses.
Require blue team to respond using normal workflows without prior detailed knowledge of attack specifics, but with awareness of the exercise scope.
Post-exercise, merge red-team logs, blue-team decisions, and system logs into a single event timeline using `analytics/merge_red_blue_timelines.ipynb`.

independent_variables: Presence vs. absence of structured exercises (tabletops, simulations, red-team engagements).
Intensity of exercises (number of scenarios, duration of simulations, complexity of red-team campaigns).
controlled_variables: Incident scenario used for baseline and post-treatment standardized simulations (same scenario config, same simulated channels, same initial conditions).
Core participant roles involved in both baseline and treatment measurements (e.g., same or equivalent job functions even if personnel change).
Measurement instruments (same surveys, same metric definitions, same analytics notebooks).
Simulation engine configuration (time compression factor, event generation logic, noise level) for baseline vs. post-treatment measurement runs.
Policies and formal playbooks in place at the start of the experiment window (changes are treated as outcomes/remediations, not preconditions).

randomization.description: If multiple teams or business units participate, randomly assign some units to run the treatment program first while others remain in baseline for a defined period, then cross over, to reduce bias due to varying maturity levels.
randomization.method: Use simple random assignment (e.g., Python’s `random.shuffle`) over the list of eligible teams, ensuring similar size and function across baseline-first and treatment-first groups.

blinding.description: Full blinding is not feasible because participants know whether they are engaging in exercises. However, metric calculation can be blinded by having an analyst who was not a participant compute and review metrics using de-identified event logs (e.g., roles instead of names).

metrics.name: time_to_detect
metrics.description: Elapsed time from first simulated adversarial event (e.g., hostile post, fake article) to the moment the organization’s monitoring or participant first flags it as a potential misinformation incident.

metrics.name: time_to_first_executive_brief
metrics.description: Elapsed time from first simulated adversarial event to the moment an executive (VP-level or above) receives a structured briefing or formal notification of the incident.

metrics.name: time_to_initial_public_response
metrics.description: Elapsed time from first simulated adversarial event to the issuance of the first official external communication (statement, post, press reply) addressing the misinformation.

metrics.name: decision_clarity_score
metrics.description: Assessment of how clearly key decisions (e.g., whether to respond publicly, what channels to use, whether to involve legal/regulators) were made and attributed during the exercise, rated via standardized rubric.

metrics.name: role_clarity_score
metrics.description: Extent to which participants understood their responsibilities, decision rights, and escalation paths, rated via immediate post-exercise survey.

metrics.name: coordination_effectiveness_score
metrics.description: Expert/facilitator rating of cross-functional coordination (handoffs, information sharing, conflict resolution) using a standardized rubric.

metrics.name: policy_alignment_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of major decisions taken during the exercise that are consistent with documented policies and playbooks (e.g., escalation matrices, comms guidelines).

metrics.name: incident_resolution_quality_score
metrics.description: Composite expert rating of the final state of the simulated incident relative to plausible best case, considering containment, stakeholder communications, and residual risk.

metrics.name: exercise_insight_density
metrics.description: Number of concrete, actionable improvement items (e.g., playbook changes, tooling gaps, training needs) identified per hour of exercise time, as recorded in AAR documents.

metrics.name: perceived_readiness_delta
metrics.description: Change in self-reported readiness between baseline and post-treatment standardized simulation, using identical survey questions (e.g., mean score difference).

primary.description: Median time_to_detect and time_to_first_executive_brief improve by at least 25% from baseline to post-treatment standardized simulation for the same scenario configuration.
primary.measurement_window: Compare baseline standardized simulation run to post-treatment standardized simulation run within 2–6 weeks after exercise program completion.

primary.description: Decision_clarity_score and coordination_effectiveness_score increase by at least 1 point on the 1–5 scale between baseline and post-treatment runs.
primary.measurement_window: Immediate debrief ratings after baseline and post-treatment standardized simulations.

secondary.description: Policy_alignment_rate improves by at least 20 percentage points between baseline and post-treatment standardized simulations.
secondary.measurement_window: Same scenario, same metrics across baseline and post-treatment runs.

secondary.description: Exercise_insight_density averages at least 2 actionable improvements per exercise hour across all tabletop, simulation, and red-team events.
secondary.measurement_window: Aggregate across all exercises conducted in the treatment program.

secondary.description: Perceived_readiness_delta is positive, with an average increase of at least 0.5 on the 1–5 scale across participants.
secondary.measurement_window: Compare post-briefing survey after baseline with post-survey after final standardized simulation.

statistical_considerations.description: Where sample sizes allow (e.g., multiple teams or repeated runs), compute simple pre/post effect sizes and non-parametric tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank) on key metrics, noting p-values with appropriate caveats. The primary goal is operationally meaningful deltas, not formal hypothesis testing.
statistical_considerations.minimum_sample_recommendation: At least one baseline and one post-treatment standardized simulation per participating team; ideally 3+ teams for cross-team comparison.

failure_modes.name: Simulation Not Representative
failure_modes.description: The chosen scenarios and simulation parameters do not reflect the organization’s true risk profile or channels, leading to misleading conclusions about readiness.
mitigations: Use the chapter’s scenario-design guidance to align scenarios with identified crown-jewel trust assets and actual channel mix.
Pilot scenarios with a small group and refine before full-scale exercises.

failure_modes.name: Overfitting to Specific Scenarios
failure_modes.description: Teams learn to handle only the exact simulated scenarios rather than underlying patterns, causing an illusion of readiness.
mitigations: Rotate scenario types (e.g., deepfake executive video, synthetic reviews, fabricated safety incident).
During debriefs, emphasize transferable principles and decision frameworks over scenario-specific facts.

failure_modes.name: Measurement Bias and Hawthorne Effects
failure_modes.description: Participants behave differently because they know they are being observed or because the exercise is labeled as an evaluation.
mitigations: Frame exercises as learning opportunities rather than performance tests.
Use consistent measurement instruments and, where possible, anonymize response and survey data in analysis.

failure_modes.name: Tooling and Technical Issues
failure_modes.description: Simulation scripts or data pipelines fail, causing delays, incomplete logs, or inconsistent event timing.
mitigations: Dry-run all scripts in a test environment before official exercises.
Maintain simple, manual fallbacks (e.g., slide decks or printed inject cards) for tabletop if automation fails.
Version-control all scenario configs and keep a log of any manual adjustments during the exercise.

failure_modes.name: Scope Creep and Participant Fatigue
failure_modes.description: Exercises try to cover too many objectives or last too long, causing rushed decisions and disengagement.
mitigations: Limit each exercise to 2–3 clearly defined objectives (e.g., test escalation, test comms alignment).
Time-box sessions and build in scheduled breaks.
Distribute exercises over several weeks rather than compressing all into a single multi-day event where possible.

failure_modes.name: Psychological Safety and Blame
failure_modes.description: Participants feel judged or blamed for decisions made under simulated pressure, reducing candor and learning.
mitigations: Establish and repeat ground rules emphasizing learning and system improvement, not individual evaluation.
Separate performance reviews from exercise participation.
Use the AAR format to focus on ‘what’ and ‘why’ rather than ‘who’.

technical: Python 3.10+ environment with standard data libraries (e.g., pandas, numpy, matplotlib) and Jupyter Notebook or JupyterLab.
Access to the repository `https://github.com/bookauthority/defending-brand-trust-ai-misinformation` cloned locally or accessible in a secure environment.
Ability to execute provided scripts/notebooks under `simulations/`, `scenarios/`, `redteam/`, and `analytics/` directories.
Internal collaboration tools for live simulations (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams, email, ticketing/incident system).
Secure storage for exercise logs, AAR documents, and metrics outputs (e.g., a restricted SharePoint, Git repo, or internal wiki).
organizational: Executive sponsorship and explicit approval for running simulated incidents and red-team activities, with clear scope and rules of engagement.
Agreed participation from core functions: communications/brand, risk, security, legal, and relevant business units.
Documented baseline policies and playbooks for incident response, even if incomplete, to compare against practice.
Time allocation for preparation, exercises, and debriefs, ideally over a 4–8 week window.
constraints_and_safety: All simulated content must be clearly labeled as synthetic and must not be posted to public channels without explicit legal and executive approval.
Red-team activities must operate only in sandbox environments or with synthetic data; no targeting of real customers, investors, or regulators.
Data privacy and confidentiality policies must be observed; logs and AARs may contain sensitive information and should be appropriately access-controlled.

run_instructions: Set Up Environment
Clone the repository: `git clone https://github.com/bookauthority/defending-brand-trust-ai-misinformation.git`.
Create and activate a virtual environment (e.g., `python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate` or equivalent on Windows).
Install required Python dependencies from the repo’s `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`: `pip install -r requirements.txt`.
Launch JupyterLab or Jupyter Notebook in the repo root: `jupyter lab` or `jupyter notebook`.
Configure Baseline Scenario
Navigate to the `scenarios/` directory and select one standardized scenario file to serve as the baseline/post-treatment common test (e.g., `scenarios/deepfake_exec_call.yaml`).
Open `simulations/baseline_run.ipynb` (or equivalent) and set the `SCENARIO_FILE` variable to the chosen scenario.
Configure time compression factor (e.g., 1 simulated hour = 5 real minutes) and output log path (e.g., `data/logs/baseline/`).
Run Baseline Simulation and Collect Metrics
Brief participants on the purpose of the baseline run and ground rules, but do not provide detailed scenario specifics.
Start the simulation from within the notebook or via CLI (`python simulations/baseline_run.py --scenario scenarios/deepfake_exec_call.yaml`).
Have participants respond using their standard tools and workflows; facilitators record key decisions and timestamps in the provided logging template (`exercises/logging_templates/decision_log.csv`).

At simulation end, run `analytics/compute_metrics.ipynb` with input paths pointing to the generated logs and decision records to calculate baseline metrics (e.g., `time_to_detect`, `decision_clarity_score`).
Administer the baseline readiness survey using `exercises/surveys/readiness_survey_template.md` or an equivalent form tool, and store responses in `data/surveys/baseline/`.
Execute Treatment Program: Tabletop Exercises, Live Simulation, Red Team
TABLETOP: Use `exercises/tabletop_guides/executive_tabletop_checklist.md` to plan an executive tabletop based on a different but related scenario (e.g., `scenarios/fake_safety_incident.yaml`).
Run the tabletop exercise, introducing injects manually or via the facilitator notebook (`exercises/facilitator_console.ipynb`). Record events and decisions using the logging template.

LIVE SIMULATION: Configure and run `simulations/live_timeline_sim.ipynb` with a scenario like `scenarios/review_bombing_campaign.yaml`, mapping injects to internal channels. Capture full logs and generate a reconstructed timeline via `analytics/build_timeline.ipynb`.

RED TEAM: Agree rules of engagement using `redteam/roe_template.md`. Generate synthetic adversarial content via `redteam/generator.ipynb` and conduct the scoped red-team exercise in sandboxed environments. Merge red and blue logs using `analytics/merge_red_blue_timelines.ipynb`.
After each exercise, complete an AAR using `exercises/debrief_templates/aar_template.md`, capturing improvement actions and updating any relevant playbooks or escalation matrices.
Re-Run Standardized Simulation for Post-Treatment Measurement

After completing the treatment program (ideally within 4–6 weeks), re-run the same standardized scenario used in the baseline, with identical configuration (same `SCENARIO_FILE`, same time compression, same logging format).
Use the same or equivalent roles for participation; brief them as before without detailed scenario walkthrough.
Execute the simulation and record decisions and timestamps using the same logging templates.
Run `analytics/compute_metrics.ipynb` again, tagging outputs as post-treatment (e.g., `data/metrics/post_treatment/`).
Administer the same readiness survey and store results in `data/surveys/post_treatment/`.
Analyze and Compare Results
Open `analytics/compare_pre_post.ipynb` and configure paths to baseline and post-treatment metrics and survey outputs.

Generate comparative plots and tables for key metrics: `time_to_detect`, `time_to_first_executive_brief`, `decision_clarity_score`, `coordination_effectiveness_score`, `policy_alignment_rate`, and `perceived_readiness_delta`.
Interpret results against the `success_criteria`; highlight areas of significant improvement and areas where metrics did not change or worsened.
Summarize findings and recommended remediation actions in an executive-ready report using the template at `exercises/reporting/executive_summary_template.md`.

run_id.description: Unique identifier for the simulation run (e.g., UUID).

scenario_id.description: Identifier of the scenario configuration used (e.g., filename or slug).

participant_id.description: Pseudonymous identifier to allow analysis without exposing names.

function.description: Organizational function or department (e.g., Communications, Legal, Security, Risk).

events.description: Chronological log of simulated adversarial events and injects.

channel.description: Simulated channel (e.g., social_twitter_like, messaging_app, news_site, internal_chat).

event_type.description: Type of inject (e.g., initial_attack_post, amplification, regulator_inquiry, employee_question).

payload_ref.description: Reference to payload content (e.g., file path or object key); content itself may be stored separately.

decisions.description: Chronological log of key decisions taken by participants during the run.

description.description: Brief natural-language summary of the decision.

policy_reference.description: Identifier of policy or playbook section referenced (if any), or 'none'.

survey_id.description: Identifier for the survey instrument (e.g., readiness_v1).

run_id.description: Identifier of the associated exercise or simulation run.

participant_id.description: Pseudonymous participant identifier matching the simulation_run record.

responses.description: Key-value pairs of question IDs to numeric or categorical responses.

improvement_items.description: Concrete, actionable follow-ups derived from the exercise.

owner_function.description: Function accountable for remediation (e.g., Communications, Security, Legal).
